terms.job: identity: name, job, origin, what someone is like
terms.trap: English speakers use ser for every 'be', including location
terms.scene: introducing yourself to a new coworker
terms.why_fields: anti_example: 'soy en…' for location is a top early mistake

terms.job: location and how someone is right now
terms.scene: phone call from the bus: where are you?
terms.why_fields: mental_model: one image fixes the ser/estar split; anti_example: the feeling trap is the #1 one

terms.trap: '¿dónde hay el baño?' for a specific, known place
terms.scene: asking a stranger for a pharmacy nearby
terms.why_fields: anti_example: hay vs está for a known thing is a real trap

terms.job: negation with no before the verb, doubled with nada/nadie/nunca
terms.trap: 'no quiero algo' calqued from 'I don't want anything'
terms.scene: declining more food at a friend's dinner
terms.why_fields: anti_example: English single negative produces 'algo' instead of 'nada'

terms.job: want a thing or to do something
terms.trap: not knowing querer also means love a person
terms.why_fields: discussion: the 'te quiero' job is useful and not a near-miss

terms.job: can: able to or allowed to
terms.trap: poder for learned skills where Spanish uses saber
terms.scene: asking someone to open the window in a hot room
terms.why_fields: anti_example: 'can you swim' → saber is a real English-caused trap
anti_example: the missing que is what learners actually produce

terms.job: going to: plans and near future
terms.scene: texting a friend about weekend plans
terms.why_fields: discussion: it is the default spoken future; the dropped a fits there briefly

terms.job: saying what you like (thing liked is the subject)
terms.why_fields: mental_model: 'it pleases me' flips the structure; anti_example: 'yo gusto' is universal

terms.job: so / then: moving a story or idea forward
terms.scene: telling why you were late to work
terms.why_fields: discussion: the stand-alone '¿Entonces?' use is common in chat
